def codons(sequence_file):
    """A function that reads a fasta file and returns a list of codons for each sequence in the file"""
    
    # First we read the fasta file and store the sequences as a string
    sequence = ""
    
    # Open the file
    with open(sequence_file) as fasta_file:
        # Read the file line by line
        for row in fasta_file:
            # If the line starts with '>', it is a header and we skip it
            if not row.startswith('>'):
                # If the line does not start with '>', it is a sequence and we add it to the list
                sequence += row.strip()
    
    # Now we split the sequences into codons
    sequence_codon_list = []
    
    # Loop over the sequence in steps of 3
    for i in range(0, len(sequence), 3):
        # Append the codon to the list if it is a full codon (3 nucleotides)
        if i + 3 <= len(sequence):
            # Then append the codon to the list
            sequence_codon_list.append(sequence[i:i + 3])
    
    # Return the list of codons
    return sequence_codon_list

title: Practical 1: Raw Read Data and Quality Control
text:
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies generate millions of short DNA sequences called reads. You’ve already become quite familiar with Nanopore sequencing by this point, and are aware that NGS reads are error-prone. Hence it is essential that before we do any further sequence analysis, we first assess the quality of our read data using command line tools that provide both efficiency and reproducibility.
In this practical, we’ll use command line tools to perform quality assessment and filtering, followed by taxonomic classification to understand what organisms are present in our samples. We will provide short-read files for you to use, as well as the code needed to perform the analyses. However, you will need to adapt paths and filenames to your own working environment, as well as select your own data and think about the biological significance of the results.

By the end of this practical, you will be able to:

Understand the structure and format of raw sequencing data (FASTQ files)
Use fastp for integrated quality assessment and filtering
Interpret quality control metrics and HTML reports
Apply quality trimming and adapter removal in a single step
Perform taxonomic classification using kraken2 in a Singularity container

Key metrics to examine in the HTML reports:

Read quality: Before and after filtering quality distributions
Base content: Per-position base composition
Adapter content: Automatic adapter detection and removal
Filtering results: Number of reads removed and why
Insert size: The size of the DNA fragments sequenced (between the adapters and paired reads combined)







Key Questions

What was the main reason for read filtering?
How did the quality distributions change after filtering?
Were any adapters detected and removed?



In some cases, you may want to customize the filtering parameters, such as hard-trimming a specific number of bases from the start or end of reads, or setting a minimum read length. You can do this by adding additional flags to the fastp command. For example, a good agnostic approach is to trim to a fixed quality threshold at the 3’ end of the reads, and filter out any reads that are too short after trimming.

section: HPC job script for kraken2 classification
text:
HPC job script for kraken2 classification
Lets begin by creating the job script that we will submit to the HPC cluster. Make sure to adjust paths to your actual directories and database locations. You can either create and edit the file on the cluster, or create it locally and then upload it to the cluster if you want. ALso this jobscript will allow you to run a single sample at a time, so you will need to change the sample name for each run, or make a loop to run multiple samples if you feel up for it.
# Create SLURM job script for kraken2 analysis

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -A C3SE408-25-2
#SBATCH -J kraken2_job
#SBATCH -p vera
#SBATCH -N 1 --cpus-per-task=12 # Request 1 node with 12 CPUs
#SBATCH -t 01:00:00
#SBATCH --output=/cephyr/users/ktor/Vera/practical_1/logs/kraken2_%j.out  # Standard output
#SBATCH --error=/cephyr/users/ktor/Vera/practical_1/logs/kraken2_%j.err   # Standard error

# Set paths - ADJUST THESE TO YOUR ACTUAL PATHS
CONTAINER_PATH="/cephyr/NOBACKUP/groups/n2bin_gu/BIO511/singularity_images/kraken2.sif"
DB_PATH="/cephyr/NOBACKUP/groups/n2bin_gu/BIO511/ref_dbs/kraken2db"
DATA_PATH="/cephyr/NOBACKUP/groups/n2bin_gu/BIO511/data/fastq"
RESULTS_PATH="/cephyr/NOBACKUP/groups/n2bin_gu/teachers/Tor/results"

# Bind paths for container
export SINGULARITY_BINDPATH="${DB_PATH}:/db,${DATA_PATH}:/data,${RESULTS_PATH}:/results"

# Create results directory
mkdir -p ${RESULTS_PATH}

# Identify sample
sample="A210"
echo "Processing sample: ${sample}"

# Run Kraken2 classification
srun singularity exec ${CONTAINER_PATH} kraken2 \
        --db /db \
        --threads 8 \
        --paired \
        --output /results/${sample}_kraken2_output.txt \
        --report /results/${sample}_kraken2_report.txt \
        --classified-out /results/${sample}_classified#.fastq \
        --unclassified-out /results/${sample}_unclassified#.fastq \
        /data/${sample}_R1.fastq.gz /data/${sample}_R2.fastq.gz

echo "Completed classification for ${sample}"

echo "All samples processed successfully"

title: Practical 3: Functional Annotation of Whole Genomes
text:
Annotation is the process of taking assembled genome sequences (or in some cases unassembled sequences) and identifying genomic features such as genes, coding sequences (CDS), tRNAs, rRNAs, and other functional elements. This is a critical step in guiding deeper analysis, as the annotated genes become guidemarks for functional identification and characterizing phenotypes. It is also typically the first step before more advanced downstream analysis after we’ve finished assembly and polishing. With annotated genomes, we can perform comparative genomics, functional profiling, and pangenome analyses.

Prokka with curated proteins
For the second run, we’ll enhance the annotation by providing Prokka with a curated set of reference proteins. This can help improve the accuracy of gene predictions and functional annotations, The curated proteins used for this ref are a collection of reference genomes for E. coli from NCBI RefSeq, which have been manually reviewed and merged. Using these curated proteins can help reduce the number of hypothetical proteins and improve the functional annotations of genes in our genome.
Strains:

Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655 (GCF_000005845.2)
Escherichia coli O157:H7 str. Sakai (GCF_000008865.2)
Escherichia coli ATCC 25922 (GCF_000401755.1)
Escherichia coli O25b:H4-ST131 (GCF_024918415.1)

text:
3 Main Concepts

Remote: a copy of your repository hosted elsewhere (e.g., GitHub). The default name is origin.
Tracking branch: a local branch that remembers which remote branch it tracks (set with git push -u origin main).
Merge vs fast‑forward: a merge creates a new commit that combines two histories; a fast‑forward just moves a pointer.
Conflict markers: lines Git writes inside a file to show both sides of a conflicting change — you edit the file to the final content and remove the markers.
Annotated tag: a named label on a commit with a message and metadata, perfect for submissions/releases.







Did You Know?



git pull ≈ git fetch + git merge. Prefer git fetch first when learning, so you can inspect before merging.

text:
4 Merge Conflict
We’ll create a tiny conflict on one line, fix it, and finish the merge.
1) Change on main
git switch -c main 2>/dev/null || git switch main
echo "genome_id: ST400" > config/config.yml
git add config/config.yml
git commit -m "Set genome_id to ST400 on main"
2) Different change on a new branch
git switch -c feature/alt-genome
echo "genome_id: ST401" > config/config.yml
git add config/config.yml
git commit -m "Set genome_id to ST401 on feature branch"
3) Merge back into main (conflict expected)
git switch main
git merge feature/alt-genome
Open config/config.yml — you’ll see markers like:
<<<<<<< HEAD
genome_id: ST400
=======
genome_id: ST401
>>>>>>> feature/alt-genome
4) Fix the file
Decide the final line (e.g., keep genome_id: ST401). Delete the three marker lines (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>). Save.
5) Tell Git you fixed it and complete the merge
git add config/config.yml
git commit   # completes the merge
Checkpoint
git log --oneline --decorate --graph -n 5






Common Mistake



Leaving conflict markers in the file (the <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> lines) will confuse you later. Remove them all before committing.

6 Share to GitHub — HTTPS or SSH

6.1 Option 1 — HTTPS

Create an empty GitHub repo named git-lab (do not add a README).

Connect your local repo (replace YOURUSER):

git remote add origin https://github.com/YOURUSER/git-lab.git
git remote -v

Push main and set tracking (you’ll sign in or use a token the first time):

git push -u origin main

Common Mistake



If you accidentally created the GitHub repo with a README, run git pull once before your first push.




6.2 Option 2 — SSH (BONUS SECTION)
This is a one‑time setup per machine. Use it if you prefer entering a passphrase once and pushing without tokens.
Step 1 — Do you already have a key?
ls -al ~/.ssh
# If you see id_ed25519 and id_ed25519.pub, you likely already have a key.
Step 2 — Create a key (if needed)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"
# Press Enter to accept the default location (~/.ssh/id_ed25519)
# Choose a passphrase (recommended) or press Enter for none
Step 3 — Add the key to your ssh-agent
# Start the agent (if not running) and add your key
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
Step 4 — Copy your PUBLIC key and add it on GitHub
# macOS: copy to clipboard
pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# If pbcopy isn't available, print and copy manually:
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
On GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → paste → Save.
Step 5 — Test your SSH connection
ssh -T git@github.com
# Expect a greeting like: "Hi <username>! You've successfully authenticated..."
Step 6 — Switch your remote from HTTPS to SSH and push
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:YOURUSER/git-lab.git
git remote -v
git push -u origin main
git push --tags






Common Mistakes




Don’t paste your private key; paste the .pub file only.

“Repository not found”? Check the username/repo and that it exists.

Locked‑down networks may block SSH — switch back to HTTPS if needed: git remote set-url origin https://github.com/YOURUSER/git-lab.git

title: Best Practices 1: Algorithmic Thinking
text:
By this point in the course you have been introduced to the basics of programming through bash, but you have not yet been introduced to the more advanced algorithms that are used in bioinformatics. In this practical, instead of simple questions like “how do i write this loop”, we now ask a deeper question:
What kind of problem is this, and what kind of algorithm is powerful enough to solve it at genomic scale?
Modern bioinformatics depends on a small number of recurring algorithmic ideas. Sequence alignment, read mapping, genome assembly, gene prediction, taxonomic classification, and variant calling all look different on the surface, but many of them reuse the same patterns:

break a biological object into computable pieces
score many possible explanations
search efficiently through a huge space of possibilities
use data structures that avoid scanning everything
accept tradeoffs between exactness, speed, memory, and biological realism







Learning Objectives



By the end of this practical, you should be able to:

Explain why naive algorithms often fail on genomic-scale data
Recognize common genomics algorithms and the problems they solve
Reflect on algorithmic tradeoffs: exact vs heuristic, fast vs sensitive, memory-efficient vs simple
Design pseudocode to describe your approach to solving a problem before writing the code

title: Best Practices 1: Algorithmic Thinking
text:
Algorithmic Vocabulary







Concept
Meaning in practice




Input
The data the algorithm starts with, such as reads, sequences, or tables


Output
The result, such as an alignment, assembly, variant list, or classification


State
Information retained by the algorithm in the background


Score
A number/metric used to compare the possible solutions given by algorithm


Search space
All possible solutions the algorithm could consider


Complexity
How runtime or memory grows as input grows


Exact algorithm
Guaranteed to find the optimal answer under its model


Heuristic algorithm
Faster strategy that may approximate or miss some answers


Dynamic programming
A method that breaks a problem into smaller subproblems and reuses their solutions


Data structure
A special organization of data that makes some operations efficient



In genomics, the most important question is often not “can I solve this for one sequence?” but “can I compute my full dataset within a reasonable time and memory usage?” The correct algorithmic choice depends on the biological question, the data type, and the scale of the problem.

title: Best Practices 1: Algorithmic Thinking
text:
Exact String Matching and k-mers
One of the simplest genomics algorithms is exact string matching: finding where a DNA pattern occurs in a longer sequence.
Question: Where does the pattern ATG occur in a genome, and which short sequence words occur most often?
Naive algorithm:
For each position in the genome:
    Compare the pattern to the genome at that position
    If all characters match:
        Report the position
genome="TTGATGCCCATGAAATGA"
pattern="ATG"

matches=''

for (( i=0; i<=${#genome}-${#pattern}; i++ )); do
    if [[ ${genome:i:${#pattern}} == $pattern ]]; then
        matches+="$(($i+1)) "
    fi
done

echo "Pattern $pattern occurs at positions: $matches"
This is fine for a small genome and a short pattern. But large-scale genomics often uses k-mers, fixed-length sequence words, to make matching faster. These are constructed by sliding a window of length k across the sequence, moving one base at a time.
sequence="ATGACCATGATTACGCCAAGCT"
k=3

for (( i=0; i<=${#sequence}-k; i++ )); do
    kmer=${sequence:i:k}
    echo $kmer
done
k-mers are used in many genomics tools:

read error correction
genome assembly
metagenomic classification
contamination checks
As sequence variation representations (similar to SNPs, but for short sequences)







Exercise



Since kmers only move one base at a time, there is typically a lot of redudancy and duplicates. Write bash code that counts all 4-mers in this sequence:
sequence="ATGACCATGATTACGCCAAGCT"
Then answer:

Which 4-mer occurs most often?
What would happen if k were very small (think 1 or 2-mers)?
What would happen if k were larger than the read length?

[Hint: Try and pipe the output of the k-mer loop with a combination of sort and uniq to count the unique k-mers.]


The key idea is that in bioinformatics, we often use sequence representations that arent necessarily biologically meaningful by themselves, but are computationally useful. k-mers are a good example of this: they are not genes, proteins, or regulatory elements or SNPs, but they are a convenient way to represent sequences for many algorithms and can be analysed to find biologically meaningful patterns.

title: Best Practices 1: Algorithmic Thinking
text:
Sequence Alignment with Dynamic Programming
The first genomics algorithm we will look at is sequence alignment. In principle it is as simple as what we did for exact string matching, but in practice it is more complicated because we need to allow for substitutions, insertions, and deletions when comparing one or more sequences.
Question: How do we compare two sequences when they may contain substitutions, insertions, and deletions?
For example:
Sequence A: A C G T A C
Sequence B: A C - T G C
The challenge is that many alignments are possible. A brute-force search over all alignments becomes impossible as sequence length grows.
Dynamic programming solves this by breaking the alignment into smaller subproblems and storing their scores in a matrix.
Well known algorithms:



Algorithm
Use




Needleman-Wunsch
Global alignment of two full sequences


Smith-Waterman
Local alignment of best matching subsequences


Viterbi
Most likely path through a hidden Markov model



For global alignment, define:
score[i][j] = best alignment score between the first i bases of sequence A
              and the first j bases of sequence B
At each cell, the algorithm chooses among three possibilities:
diagonal: align A[i] with B[j]
up:       align A[i] with a gap
left:     align B[j] with a gap
Simplified recurrence:
score[i][j] = max(
    score[i-1][j-1] + match_or_mismatch,
    score[i-1][j]   + gap_penalty,
    score[i][j-1]   + gap_penalty
)
This is algorithmically sophisticated because the method does not try every full alignment independently. It reuses partial solutions. Runtime is still usually proportional to the product of sequence lengths, O(nm), but that is far better than enumerating all possible alignments.






Biological Interpretation



The scoring system is a biological model. A high match score says matches are likely or valuable. A strong gap penalty says insertions/deletions are costly. Changing the scoring scheme changes what kind of alignment the algorithm prefers.

title: Best Practices 1: Algorithmic Thinking
section: Read Mapping with Indexes, BWT, and FM-index
text:
Read Mapping with Indexes, BWT, and FM-index
Question: Where did each sequencing read most likely come from in the reference genome?
A naive mapper compares every read to every genome position. Modern mappers avoid this by building an index of the reference genome.
Well known ideas and tools:







Idea
Used for




suffix arrays
fast substring search


Burrows-Wheeler Transform (BWT)
compressed representation that preserves searchable structure


FM-index
memory-efficient exact matching based on BWT


BWA and Bowtie
widely used read mappers based on these ideas



Conceptual algorithm:
Build an index of the reference genome
For each read:
    Search for exact seed matches using the index
    Extend or refine candidate matches
    Score candidate alignments
    Report the best location or mark the read as ambiguous
The cleverness is in the index. Instead of storing every possible alignment, the algorithm stores the reference in a form that supports fast backward search.
This is why read mapping can be feasible even when there are millions of reads. The expensive work is partly shifted into building an efficient reference index.






Code example





This code shows the core idea behind BWT/FM-index searching. It builds a suffix array, creates a Burrows-Wheeler Transform, and uses backward search to find exact matches.
def suffix_array(text):
    return sorted(range(len(text)), key=lambda position: text[position:])


def burrows_wheeler_transform(text):
    if not text.endswith("$"):
        text = text + "$"

    sa = suffix_array(text)
    bwt = []

    for position in sa:
        if position == 0:
            bwt.append(text[-1])
        else:
            bwt.append(text[position - 1])

    return "".join(bwt), sa, text


def build_fm_index(bwt):
    alphabet = sorted(set(bwt))
    running_counts = {}

    for character in alphabet:
        running_counts[character] = 0

    occ = []
    for character in bwt:
        occ.append(running_counts.copy())
        running_counts[character] = running_counts[character] + 1
    occ.append(running_counts.copy())

    first_column_start = {}
    total = 0
    for character in alphabet:
        first_column_start[character] = total
        total = total + running_counts[character]

    return first_column_start, occ


def fm_index_positions(pattern, bwt, suffix_array_values, first_column_start, occ):
    top = 0
    bottom = len(bwt)

    for character in reversed(pattern):
        if character not in first_column_start:
            return []

        top = first_column_start[character] + occ[top][character]
        bottom = first_column_start[character] + occ[bottom][character]

        if top >= bottom:
            return []

    return sorted(suffix_array_values[top:bottom])


reference = "GATTACAGATTACA"
bwt, sa, indexed_text = burrows_wheeler_transform(reference)
first_column_start, occ = build_fm_index(bwt)

print(indexed_text)
print(bwt)
print(fm_index_positions("TACA", bwt, sa, first_column_start, occ))

title: Best Practices 1: Algorithmic Thinking
section: Hidden Markov Models for predicting genes and proteins
text:
Hidden Markov Models for predicting genes and proteins
Further along when working with genomic pipelines, we typically want to predict what biological meaning the sequences have. For example, we may want to predict which parts of a genome are coding, which parts are intergenic, and which parts are regulatory. There are many ways to do this, such as likelihood-based predicitions or HMMs, for now we will focus on HMMs.
Question: Given an observed DNA or protein sequence, what hidden biological states most likely generated it?
A hidden Markov model, or HMM, is useful when the observed data are visible but the underlying biological state is hidden.
Example:
Observed sequence: A T G G C A T A A ...
Hidden state:      intergenic, start codon, coding region, stop codon, ...
An HMM includes:

states, such as coding and non-coding
transition probabilities between states
emission probabilities for observed bases or amino acids

The Viterbi algorithm finds the most likely sequence of hidden states.
Conceptual pseudocode:
For each position in the sequence:
    For each possible hidden state:
        Calculate the best score for arriving at this state
        Store where that best score came from
Trace back from the best final state to recover the most likely path
HMMs appear in:

gene prediction
protein domain detection
profile HMM searches, such as HMMER
annotation of conserved protein families

HMMs are powerful because they let us model biological uncertainty. Instead of saying “this position definitely is coding”, the algorithm asks which hidden explanation is most probable under the model.






Code example





This toy HMM has two hidden states: coding and noncoding. The observed data are DNA bases. The Viterbi algorithm finds the most likely hidden-state path.
import math


def log_probability(value):
    return math.log(value)


def viterbi(observations, states, start_probability, transition_probability, emission_probability):
    dynamic_table = []
    backpointer = []

    first_column = {}
    first_backpointer = {}

    for state in states:
        first_column[state] = (
            log_probability(start_probability[state]) +
            log_probability(emission_probability[state][observations[0]])
        )
        first_backpointer[state] = None

    dynamic_table.append(first_column)
    backpointer.append(first_backpointer)

    for position in range(1, len(observations)):
        column = {}
        column_backpointer = {}

        for current_state in states:
            best_previous_state = None
            best_score = None

            for previous_state in states:
                score = (
                    dynamic_table[position - 1][previous_state] +
                    log_probability(transition_probability[previous_state][current_state]) +
                    log_probability(emission_probability[current_state][observations[position]])
                )

                if best_score is None or score > best_score:
                    best_score = score
                    best_previous_state = previous_state

            column[current_state] = best_score
            column_backpointer[current_state] = best_previous_state

        dynamic_table.append(column)
        backpointer.append(column_backpointer)

    final_state = max(dynamic_table[-1], key=dynamic_table[-1].get)
    best_path = [final_state]

    for position in range(len(observations) - 1, 0, -1):
        final_state = backpointer[position][final_state]
        best_path.append(final_state)

    best_path.reverse()
    return best_path


states = ["coding", "noncoding"]
start_probability = {"coding": 0.5, "noncoding": 0.5}
transition_probability = {
    "coding": {"coding": 0.90, "noncoding": 0.10},
    "noncoding": {"coding": 0.10, "noncoding": 0.90}
}
emission_probability = {
    "coding": {"A": 0.20, "T": 0.20, "G": 0.30, "C": 0.30},
    "noncoding": {"A": 0.30, "T": 0.30, "G": 0.20, "C": 0.20}
}

print(viterbi("ATGGCGC", states, start_probability, transition_probability, emission_probability))

text:
In this course you will use the command line and the Vera high performance computing cluster for bioinformatics work. Before setting up accounts, VPN, SSH, and VSCode, it helps to understand what kind of system Vera is and how work is expected to run on it.
This lecture is based on the C3SE introduction to Vera and the C3SE Vera system overview. It is written for master’s students in chemistry and molecular biology who may be new to shared computing systems.






Learning objectives



By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

Explain what an HPC cluster is in plain language.
Describe the difference between a login node and a compute node.
Explain why jobs are submitted to a scheduler instead of run directly.
Recognize the most important resources: CPU cores, RAM, storage, time, GPUs, and VRAM.
Understand the basic workflow for running work on Vera.
Know where the later “Setting up the HPC” practical fits into the bigger picture.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
text:
CPU
The CPU is the general-purpose processor in a computer. It is good at running the operating system, scripts, command line tools, and most standard bioinformatics programs. When a SLURM job asks for “cores”, it is asking for CPU cores.
Examples of CPU-heavy work:

Running bwa, samtools, blast, fastqc, or many Python/R scripts.
Sorting large tables.
Running many independent sample analyses in parallel.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
text:
GPU
The GPU is a specialised accelerator originally designed for graphics, but now also used for many scientific and machine learning tasks. A GPU can do some kinds of numerical work very quickly, especially when the software has been written to use the GPU.
Examples of GPU-aware work:

Some deep learning programs using PyTorch or TensorFlow with CUDA.
Some molecular dynamics or molecular modelling software configured for GPUs.
Some image analysis workflows.

Many ordinary command line tools do not use a GPU. If the program cannot use a GPU, requesting one will not make the job faster.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
text:
RAM
RAM is the short-term memory used by the CPU while a program is running. If a genome assembly needs to keep a large graph in memory, or a Python script loads a large matrix, that memory is RAM.
If a job runs out of RAM, it may crash or be killed by the scheduler.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
text:
VRAM
VRAM is the memory built into a GPU card. GPU programs must fit the data they process on the GPU into VRAM. This is why GPU cards are often described by both model and memory size, for example A40 with 48 GB VRAM or H100 with 96 GB VRAM.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
text:
Simplified Vera hardware
The Vera documentation currently describes two main CPU generations:








Node type
CPU hardware
Simple meaning




Zen4
2 AMD EPYC 9354 CPUs per node, 32 cores per CPU
64 CPU cores per full node; currently the default if you do not request a specific CPU type


Icelake
2 Intel Xeon Gold 6338 CPUs per node, 32 cores per CPU
64 CPU cores per full node; can be requested when needed



Standard Zen4 Vera nodes commonly have 768 GB RAM per node. Icelake nodes commonly have 512 GB RAM per node. Some nodes have more memory, such as 1024 or 1536 GB RAM, and some larger-memory nodes may be private or limited to specific projects.
The seminar slides describe Vera in terms of CPU generations and accelerator cards. The live Vera hardware page gives the exact current node counts. You do not need to memorize the numbers. The useful student-level summary is:

Most normal jobs run on 64-core CPU nodes.
Many standard nodes have hundreds of GB of RAM, far more than a laptop.
Some nodes have larger RAM for memory-hungry jobs.
A small number of nodes have GPUs, so GPU jobs are a special request.
You can inspect current node information on Vera with sinfo.

Vera also has GPU nodes:










GPU type
Approximate total on main partition
Where it is used
VRAM per GPU
Beginner-level interpretation




A40
16 GPUs
Icelake GPU nodes
about 45-48 GB
Useful for some GPU workloads, often graphics/AI-oriented


A100
12 GPUs
Icelake GPU nodes
40 GB
Strong scientific/AI GPU


H100
8 GPUs
Zen4 GPU nodes
about 94-96 GB
Very powerful newer GPU



The C3SE slides also list theoretical floating-point performance for A40, A100, and H100 GPUs. These numbers can be useful for specialists, but for this course the important message is simpler:

CPU nodes are the normal choice for most command line and bioinformatics jobs.
Large-memory nodes are useful when a program needs a lot of RAM.
GPU nodes are useful only when the software is GPU-aware.
You should not request special hardware unless you know why your job needs it.

Example GPU accounting from the C3SE slides:








GPU
Extra allocation cost
What this means




A40

Lower extra cost


A100
48 extra core-hour equivalents per GPU-hour
Higher extra cost


H100
160 extra core-hour equivalents per GPU-hour
Highest extra cost



For example, if a job uses part of a CPU node plus one A100 for 10 hours, the project is charged for the CPU cores plus the extra GPU cost. This is why GPU requests should be intentional.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
text:
Vera, Alvis, Cephyr, and Mimer
The C3SE slides mention several systems. They are related, but they are not the same thing.








Name
What it is
How it relates to Vera




Vera
The HPC compute cluster used in this course
Where your CPU/GPU jobs run


Alvis
A NAISS system for AI/ML research
A different compute system; it is retiring and being replaced by Arrhenius


Cephyr
A C3SE storage system based on CephFS
Provides storage areas used by C3SE systems, including Vera project/home storage


Mimer
A high-performance storage system based on WekaIO
Mainly intended for Alvis-style high-I/O workloads, but can also be available for data staging from other systems



In short: Vera computes; Cephyr and Mimer store data; Alvis is another compute system.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
text:
Login nodes
Login nodes are the front doors of the cluster. You use them to:

Connect to Vera.
Navigate files.
Edit scripts.
Transfer small files.
Prepare job scripts.
Submit jobs to the scheduler.
Check job status.

Login nodes are shared by many users. They are not for large calculations.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
text:
Compute nodes
Compute nodes are where heavy work runs. You use them indirectly by submitting a job. The scheduler starts your script on one or more compute nodes when the requested resources are available.
Use compute nodes for:

Genome assembly.
Mapping reads.
Large BLAST or database searches.
Long-running Python or R analyses.
Molecular simulations.
GPU-enabled workloads.







Main rule



Do not run big or long jobs on the login node. Prepare your work on the login node, then submit it to the scheduler so it can run on compute nodes.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
section: “I am logged in, so I can run my analysis here”
text:
“I am logged in, so I can run my analysis here”
Not quite. You are usually on a login node. Use it to prepare and submit work, not to run heavy analyses.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
section: “More cores always makes my job faster”
text:
“More cores always makes my job faster”
Only if the software can use multiple cores efficiently. Some programs are single-core. Giving them 32 cores will not make them 32 times faster.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
text:
“A GPU is always better”
Only GPU-aware software benefits from a GPU. Many standard command line and bioinformatics programs are CPU-based. If your program documentation does not mention CUDA, GPU acceleration, NVIDIA GPUs, or a GPU-specific option, assume it is probably CPU-based.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
section: “If my job waits, something is wrong”
text:
“If my job waits, something is wrong”
Not necessarily. Queuing is normal on shared systems. Your job may be waiting for priority, enough free resources, or a suitable node.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
section: “The cluster will keep all temporary files”
text:
“The cluster will keep all temporary files”
No. Temporary job storage such as $TMPDIR is cleaned when the job ends. Copy final results back to persistent storage.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
section: E1: Can I make my own Conda environment?
text:
E1: Can I make my own Conda environment?
Usually, yes, but on Vera it is not the first recommended option. C3SE recommends this order:

Prefer centrally installed modules when they already contain what you need.
For Python packages, prefer a Python virtualenv built on top of loaded modules.
For complex Conda environments, prefer building an Apptainer/Singularity container.
Use a direct Conda environment only when you have a clear reason and understand that it can create many files and use quota quickly.

The reason is practical: Conda environments often contain thousands of small files. On a shared network filesystem this can be slow and can use up your file quota. Containers turn the environment into one portable .sif file, which is easier for the storage system.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
section: E2: Recommended simple Python environment with virtualenv
text:
E2: Recommended simple Python environment with virtualenv
Use this when your script needs extra Python packages.
Create the environment once:
# 1. Search for suitable modules
module spider Python
module spider SciPy-bundle
module spider virtualenv

# 2. Load Python-related modules from a compatible toolchain
# The exact versions may change; use versions available on Vera.
module load virtualenv/20.26.2-GCCcore-13.3.0
module load SciPy-bundle/2024.05-gfbf-2024a

# 3. Create an environment in a project or course storage area if possible
mkdir -p /cephyr/NOBACKUP/groups/replace_with_project/my_envs
cd /cephyr/NOBACKUP/groups/replace_with_project/my_envs
virtualenv --system-site-packages bio511_env

# 4. Activate it
source bio511_env/bin/activate

# 5. Install only the extra packages you need
pip install package_name
Use the environment in a job script:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -A replace_with_project_account
#SBATCH -p vera
#SBATCH -n 4
#SBATCH -t 01:00:00
#SBATCH -J bio511_python

module purge
module load virtualenv/20.26.2-GCCcore-13.3.0
module load SciPy-bundle/2024.05-gfbf-2024a

source /cephyr/NOBACKUP/groups/replace_with_project/my_envs/bio511_env/bin/activate

python my_script.py






Avoid pip install --user



Do not install Python packages directly into ~/.local with pip install --user. Packages installed there can interfere with other environments and can quickly use up your home quota.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
section: E3: If you really need Conda
text:
E3: If you really need Conda
C3SE notes that Miniforge modules are available, but recommends using Conda inside a container for most cases. If a course instructor specifically asks you to create a Conda environment directly on Vera, the basic idea is:
# 1. Search for available Miniforge or Conda modules
module spider Miniforge
module spider conda

# 2. Load the available module shown by Vera.
# Replace <version> with the exact module version shown by `module spider`.
module load Miniforge3/<version>

# 3. Create the environment in project storage, not in your small home quota
mkdir -p /cephyr/NOBACKUP/groups/replace_with_project/conda_envs
conda create -p /cephyr/NOBACKUP/groups/replace_with_project/conda_envs/bio511_conda \
  -c conda-forge python=3.11 package_name

# 4. Activate it
conda activate /cephyr/NOBACKUP/groups/replace_with_project/conda_envs/bio511_conda

# 5. Test your script
python my_script.py
Use it in a job script by loading the same module and activating the same path before running the script.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
section: E4: Container alternative for Conda dependencies
text:
E4: Container alternative for Conda dependencies
For a complex Conda environment, a container is often better. A container recipe can install packages from an environment.yml, and the finished .sif file can be run in a job:
apptainer exec my_environment.sif python my_script.py
For GPU containers, the command usually needs --nv so the container can see NVIDIA GPUs:
apptainer exec --nv my_gpu_environment.sif python gpu_script.py
You do not need to master containers in this first HPC introduction, but you should know that they are often the cleaner alternative to large Conda environments on a shared cluster.

title: Practical 2: High performance computing clusters - intro
text:
E4: Do I need tmux?
Usually, no. For normal HPC work you should submit long-running analyses with sbatch. Once the job is submitted, it belongs to the scheduler, not to your laptop connection. You can close your computer, disconnect from VPN, or lose Wi-Fi, and the batch job should continue running.
Use this safe pattern:
sbatch job_script.sh
squeue -u $USER
Then you can log out. Later, log in again and check the output files and SLURM log.
tmux can still be useful for:

Editing files during a long login session.
Keeping a terminal layout open while you prepare scripts.
Running short monitoring commands.

But tmux is not a replacement for SLURM. Do not start a long analysis inside tmux on the login node. If you need an interactive compute session for debugging, use an interactive SLURM job or the Open OnDemand portal, and keep it short.

title: Practical 1: Introduction to Command Line Interface
text:
Doing bioinformatics often necessitates the handling of very large files, with complex structure and dense matrices. This makes them often unwieldy to pretty much impossible to handle in traditional GUI-based analysis tools (such as Excel), and as such we rely on more rudimental and lightweight file handling systems such as bash-based command line enviroments that allow us to interact with our computer on a more fundamental level.
Typically the first thing you encounter on opening a new terminal instance is:
user@computer:~$
This is the terminal prompt where you’ll be able to issue commands to the computer, with the syntax (“grammar” of the code) of your command prompts often using the following structure:
user@computer:-$ command -option my_object

# or you may have more advanced command prompts
user@computer:-$ command -threads 2 -output $My_Directory_Variable/ -prefix New_file_ -accessoryfile Additional_file my_object | nextcommand -cvfz New_file_my_object.tar.gz
Imagination (and resources, complexity, optimization…) sets the limit of what you can do in the CLI
If you’re further curious on the history of shell and the command line.






Learning Objectives



By the end of this practical, you should be able to:

Navigate the file system using cd and ls
Create and manipulate directories with mkdir
Create, copy, move, and delete files using touch, cp, mv, and rm
View file contents using cat, head, and tail
Search within files using grep
Display text using echo
Edit text using sed
Tie these commands together using pipes
Plan your computational workflow using pseudocode

title: Practical 1: Introduction to Command Line Interface
text:
Understanding Your Location (pwd and ls)
Before we start creating new things in our directory its a good idea to get a grip on your whereabouts within the working directory

pwd: Print working directory - shows your current location
ls: List contents of directories
command --help: Show help-documentation for a command, very useful for lookups when we need a command to do something specific

Find your current location and explore the directory
# Run pwd
pwd

# Run ls
ls

# Setting the -l flag for ls will give you a more detailed view of the contents of the directory
ls -l

# Run with the help flag to get the documentation for the command
pwd --help
You can also use the man command to get a more detailed manual for a command, which is especially useful for more complex commands with many options. For example, you can run man ls to see the manual for the ls command. If you have an internet connection, it is also possible to search for command documentation online, for example by searching for “ls command linux” in your preferred search engine.






Exercise: Hidden Files and Directories



Some programs make “hidden” directories and files in you directories that fulfill important functions for the program, these are usually denoted by a . in front of the name. To list these hidden files and directories we need a special option flag for the lscommand.

Use the –help flag and look through the documentation to find the right flag for ls to show hidden files and folders.







Expected output (no peeking!)





The flag for ls to show hidden files and directories is -a. You can use it like this:
ls -a

# or as a list
ls -la

title: Practical 1: Introduction to Command Line Interface
section: Making and Changing Directories (mkdir and cd)
text:
Making and Changing Directories (mkdir and cd)
Since the command line interface (CLI) can quickly become cluttered, we organize our work into directories. Similar to the folders on windows or macOS, directories act as containers that create a hierarchy of files and subdirectories. This is especially important in bioinformatics, where we often deal with large datasets and multiple analysis steps that need to be organized for reproducibility and clarity.

mkdir: Create new directories
cd: Change directory
Special directories: . (current), .. (parent), ~ (home), / (root)

Create and navigate a genomics project structure
# Create a main directory for this exercise
mkdir CLI_intro

# Navigate into it
cd CLI_intro

# Create additional directories within the main directory
# This can be done in multiple ways 
# For example, you could make multiple directories in one command:
mkdir Escherichia
cd Escherichia
mkdir coli hermanni fergusonii

# Check your structure
ls -la

# Navigate around and try the special directory short-hands
cd ~        # Go home
cd ..        # Go back to previous directory






Additional Command: tree [Optional]





There is another very useful command for visualising directories called tree, which will print the directory structure in a tree-like format. This is especially useful for visualizing complex project structures. If you don’t have it installed, you can usually install it via your package manager (e.g., sudo apt install tree on Ubuntu/WSL2 or brew install tree for MacOS).

Try running tree in your current directory to see the structure of your project. You can also use tree -L 2 to limit the depth of the tree displayed.
Sometimes we only want to see the directory structure without all the files, if you have time then look for the flag that allows you to do this in the tree documentation.

Tree is very useful for visualizing complex project structures, but it is not always installed by default and we might also not always need the amount of information it provides. Sometimes a simple ls command is enough to get a good overview of the directory structure.

title: Practical 1: Introduction to Command Line Interface
text:
Text manipulation (echo, touch, less, cat)
Before we start with file manipulation, we’ll first introduce text files the old school way via echo and touch, as well as some commands to view the contents of files.

touch: Create empty files
echo: Print text provided in the prompts
less: View file contents in a scrollable format
cat: Concatenate and display file contents

Handling text in CLI
# First, lets use echo in the ye olde intro to programming way
echo "Hello World!"

# Not the most exciting, but we can use it to add text to files via > 
# Create a file using touch 
touch test_file

# Then add some text to the file 
echo "Some_text" > test_file

# You can view the contents of the file using `cat` or `less`
cat test_file # Prints to the terminal
less test_file # Opens a scrollable instance of the file
# To exit less, press `q` on your keyboard

# Now add some more text to the next line in the file
# To add to a file you simply extend the > operator to >> 
echo "Some_more_text" >> test_file

# Now lastly, try to wipe the file with some new text
# This removes all the previous text and replaces it with the new text, but we will see that 
# In the next section.
echo "New_text" > test_file

title: Practical 1: Introduction to Command Line Interface
text:
File Manipulation (cp, mv, rm)
Now let’s create some mock files that we will use downstream in the analysis, and learn how to use commands to copy, rename and remove files

mv: Rename the absolute path of a file (moving it)
cp: Copy a file
rm: Remove a file (Irreversible, be careful!!)

Create sample files and practice file operations
# Create some more directories to store everything in 
mkdir -p raw_data backups

# Make a test file to work with
echo "This is a test file for practicing file manipulation." > test_file.txt
echo "It contains some sample text for testing purposes." >> test_file.txt

# Copy files (backup your data!)
cp test_file.txt raw_data/
cp test_file.txt test_file_backup.txt

# Move files to organize your project
mv test_file_backup.txt backups/

# remove files (be careful, no undo!)
rm test_file.txt

# rm can also be used with flags to remove directories and their contents
rm -r backups/

title: Practical 1: Introduction to Command Line Interface
text:
Text Editing with sed (Stream Editor)
If we want to make edits to lines or whole files, without having to rewrite whole files, we can use the sed command. sed sees input as a stream of text, and allows us to perform operations on it, such as find-and-replace, deletion, or insertion of text while the program reads the input line by line. This is especially useful for large files where opening them in a text editor would be impractical. The output of sed is printed to the terminal by default, but it can also be redirected to a new file with > or edited inplace with the -i flag.

sed (stream editor): Allows for edits of existing text and replacing/modifying it with new text

Use sed for find-and-replace operations
# Create a sample file for sed operations
echo "This is some old-text that needs to be replaced." > input_sed.txt

# Now run sed to replace all instances of 'old-text' with 'new-text'
sed 's/old-text/new-text/g' input_sed.txt > output_sed.txt
cat output_sed.txt

# Note that sed does not write to the original file unless you use the -i flag (in-place)
sed -i 's/old-text/new-text/g' input_sed.txt
cat input_sed.txt

# It can also be used to delete lines containing a specific pattern
sed '/plasmid/d' gene_annotations.csv > chromosomal_only.csv
cat chromosomal_only.csv






When to use sed and when to use an editor (nano, vim, etc.) (Optional)





While you’ve probably used text editors like “Notes” on you computer or more advanced word processors like Word, command line environments are typically not adequate for heavy GUI (Graphical User Interface) based applications. Instead we often use more scaled down, but still powerful, editors like nano or vim that work well in the command line environment. These editors allow for more complex text manipulation and editing, but they require a bit of a learning curve to use effectively. In this course we focus on using IDEs (Integrated Development Environments) for writing scripts and code, but for quick edits on the HPC for example, text editors like nano and stream editors like sed are very useful to learn.
Examples of when to use sed vs a text editor:








Use Case

Note



sed is one of the more dynamic tools used in the command line, and they way we have introduced it here is quite simple, as a tool for small find and replace operations. For a more in depth look at sed and its capabilities, check out some other resources like this. It is also, technically, a programming language

title: Practical 1: Introduction to Command Line Interface
section: Putting it all together with pipes (|)
text:
Putting it all together with pipes (|)
Here’s where the command line really starts to shine! Pipes allow you to chain commands together, passing the output of one command as input to another. This creates powerful, flexible operations that can process data in more advanced ways with just a single line of code. It also saves us time by not having to run multiple executions before we get our desired output.

|: Pipe - pass output from one command to another

Chaining commands together will be key later in this course section, when we start working on scripts.
Create files and use pipes for complex operations
# Skip the header and show only first 2 data rows
grep -v "Gene_ID" gene_annotations.csv | head -n 2

# We can combine commands to edit specific lines as well 
# Use it to remove all the underscores from the sequence headers in sequences.fasta
grep '^>' sequences.fasta | sed 's/_/ /g'

# Classic examples of pipes use some additional commands we havent introduced yet
# For example, we can use cut, sort and uniq to find unique gene names in the gene_annotations.csv file
cut -d',' -f1 gene_annotations.csv | sort | uniq

# One thing to keep in mind is that pipes need a "stream" of input/output.
# To understand this, test and see what happens when we direct output to file in the middle of a pipe chain
cut -d',' -f1 gene_annotations.csv | sort > sorted_genes.txt | uniq






Exercise: Pipes and edits



Using the mock genomics data you created earlier, perform the following tasks using pipes and sed:

title: Practical 1: Introduction to Command Line Interface
text:
Pseudocode for Scripts
But this becomes all the more important as we start to write scripts and programs, where we need to think about the flow of data and the sequence of operations. By writing pseudocode first, we can ensure that our analysis is well-structured and that the logic is sound before we start coding. For this the format of the pseudocode is a bit subjective, but it should clearly outline the steps of the analysis, including the input data, the processing steps, and the expected output. It should also be easy to read and understand, and make sense in the context of the target language syntax.
Pseudocode for the overarching parts of a script to analyze some genomics data
Input: 
  sequences.fasta
  reference_genome.fasta

Steps:
  read files
  align sequences to reference genome
  filter alignments based on quality
  count number of aligned sequences
  write results to output file

Output:
  alignment_results.txt
Its also a good idea to outline pseudocode for the key steps of the analysis, such as the main function used to align sequences, or the function used to filter alignments. This helps to ensure that each step of the analysis is well-defined and that the code is organized in a logical manner. Simple pseudocode for the “count number of aligned sequences” step could look like this:
for each aligned sequence:
  if alignment quality is above threshold:
    count as valid alignment
    valid_alignments += 1
  else:
    discard alignment
    Print text to terminal: "Alignment discarded due to low quality"

Print text to terminal: "Total valid alignments: " + valid_alignments

Translate the following sets of operations into pseudocode. Try to keep it simple and clear, and think about the input, process, and output for each operation.

Key Takeaways




Organization matters, good directory structure keeps your files findable, we’ll learn more about this in the next practical!

Symlinks: linking shared or large data
Up until now, the paths we have used have been the real physical paths to files/directories. However, sometimes we want to link to a ex. database without copying it. This is especially useful for large files (like reference genomes) or shared files (like annotation databases). Instead of copying the file into your project, you can create a symbolic link (symlink) that points to the original file. This way, you avoid unnecessary copies and keep one source for files needed for many things.
# Example: link a shared reference into your existing refs/ folder
cd ~
mkdir ref_db_test
cd ~/CLI_intro/refs
ln -s ~/ref_db_test ref_test_link   # create a symlink
ls -l # you should see the symlink with an arrow pointing to the original file






Exercise: What is the true path of the symlink?



Often when we run commands, we need to provide the path to a file. However, in certain cases the symlink path will break and we instead need to provide the true path to the file. cd into the refs/ directory and try to figure out a way to get the true path of the symlink you just created. Hint: pwd is useful here, but there are many ways that work.

title: Practical 3 — Workspace & Data Management
text:
Field delimiters and newlines
So by now you know quite well how to peek at files with cat and less, but we didnt talk a lot about what sits inbetween the columns in the files. Columns, or fields, are separated by a delimiter which can vary depending on the file type. You are probably familiar with .csv files, which are comma-separated and thus there is a , between each column. So to create a comma delimited file, we include a , between each column when we echo and redirect. Other examples of delimiters are:

tab (\t)
space ()
pipe (|)

To split a line into more rows its also good to know that the newline character (\n) is used to separate rows. In this segment we will create a small tab-separated file and use it to demonstrate some of the commands used to summarize data.
We will now construct a toy metadata file with 5 samples, each with a country and tissue type. The file will be tab-separated and we will use an extended echo command to create it. The -e flag expands the code to interpret \-characters like \t for tab and \n for newline. We will also use the head command to check that the file was created correctly.
cd ~/CLI_intro

# Create a small tab-separated file
echo -e 'Sample_ID\tCountry\tTissue\nS1\tSE\tgut\nS2\tSE\tgut\nS3\tNO\tskin\nS4\tDK\tgut\nS5\tSE\tskin\n' > data/metadata.tsv

# Check the file was created correctly
head data/metadata.tsv

# If you are unsure of the field delimiter, cat has a useful option to visualize it:
cat -A data/metadata.tsv   # shows tab characters (^I), as well as other hidden characters

section: Counts and quick summaries with wc, sort, uniq and cut
text:
Counts and quick summaries with wc, sort, uniq and cut
Four commands that are quite lovely in pipes are wc, sort, uniq and cut

wc counts lines, words, or characters in a file
sort orders lines according to a specified criteria (alphabetically, numerically, etc.)
uniq removes duplicates from a file, but only adjacent duplicates.
cut extracts specific columns from a file, based on a delimiter.

These can be combined in a pipeline to quickly summarize data. For example, if we want to count how many samples are from each country in our metadata file or pull out all gene annotation names from a larger file, but drop all of the info beyond gene name and annotation. However remember to sort before using uniq:





flowchart LR
    title["Correct sort/uniq order"]
    In["Unsorted Data"] --> A["sort: orders lines so duplicate aggregate"] 
    B["uniq: removes duplicates that are adjacent"] 
    C["File redirect or stdout"]
    D["uniq: removes duplicates, but miss those that are not adjacent"]
    E["Missed duplicates!"]
    A --> B
    B --> C
    In -.-> D
    D -.-> E

    classDef wrong fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#c0392b,color:#c0392b;
    class D,E wrong;    






Now lets try these commands on the metadata file we just created.
# Example: cut can be used to extract one specific column, or multiple columns
cut -f2 data/metadata.tsv              # column 2 (e.g., country) from a TAB-separated file
cut -f2,3 data/metadata.tsv            # columns 2 and 3 (e.g., country and tissue) from a TAB-separated file

# wc is also very useful to get the lenght of a file, which is good to sanity check in case there is an unexpected number of rows
wc -l data/metadata.tsv

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# However these commands are at their most iconic together
# Test them step by step here before combining into a single pipeline.
# STEP-BY-STEP :
cut -f2 data/metadata.tsv              # column 2 (e.g., country) from a TAB-separated file
cut -f2 data/metadata.tsv | sort       # order values to cluster identical ones
cut -f2 data/metadata.tsv | sort | uniq -c   # collapse adjacent duplicates and count

# Now that you’ve seen each stage, try the **pipeline** form that saves the result:

cut -f2 data/metadata.tsv | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr > results/country_counts.txt
head results/country_counts.txt






Exercise: Summarizing data and changing delimiters



Sometimes, certain programs might require data in a specific format. While we often can go back to Excel or likewise to export it in a different format, it is often more efficient to do this directly in the command line. We have now learned a bit about delimiters and how to select specific columns from a file, lets see if we can put it to good use with the commands we learned in the first practical.

Use cut to extract columns “Gene_ID”, “Chromosome” and “Product” from the gene_annotations.csv file, then use sed to change the delimiter from a comma to tab, then redirect the output to a new file called gene_annotations.tsv in the data/ folder.







Example solution (Try to solve it yourself before checking!)






# Cuts default delimiter is tab, so we need to specify the delimiter as a comma with `-d,` and select the first three columns with `-f1,2,3`. Then we use `sed` to replace commas with tabs and redirect the output to a new file.
cut -d, -f1,2,3 data/gene_annotations.csv | sed 's/,/\t/g' > data/gene_annotations.tsv

# cat -A data/gene_annotations.tsv:
Gene_ID^IChromosome^IProduct$
lacZ^Iplasmid^Ibeta-galactosidase$
rpoB^Ichr^IRNA_polymerase_beta_subunit$
gyrA^Ichr^IDNA_gyrase_subunit_A$
ompA^Ichr^Iouter_membrane_protein_A$
gyrA^Ichr^IDNA_gyrase_subunit_A$

title: Practical 3 — Workspace & Data Management
text:
Locate things with find
It all happens to us eventually, we forget where we put a file or we want to find all files of a certain type. The find command is very useful for this. It can search for files based on name, type, size, and many other criteria. It is also quite useful in automated scripts, for bioinformatics it is especially useful in scripts meant for batch processing of many files. We will cover more on scripts in Practical 4, but for now lets see some examples of how to use find to locate files.






A note on regex and wildcards





find and a lot of other commands benefit from expanded use with regex (regular expressions) and wildcards. For example,

* matches any number of characters,
? matches a single character, and
[abc] matches any one of the characters a, b, or c. 

These can be combined to create powerful search patterns with find. For example, *.tsv will match all files that end with .tsv, while data/*[0-9].csv will match all CSV files in the data directory that end with a digit. Other commands like grep and sed also use regex and wildcards, so it is worth learning more about them as you become more comfortable with the command line.



cd ~/CLI_intro

# all TSV files, we use the `*` wildcard to match any characters before the `.tsv` extension
find . -name "*.tsv"

# We can also search for large files specifically, to not get crowded by small config files
# Note that M = 1024*1024 bytes, so +1M means files larger than 1 MB, similarity G = 1024*1024*1024 bytes, so +1G means files larger than 1 GB
find data -type f -size +1M    

# Sometimes we want to limit depth as well, ex. if we only want a current directory and its subs
find . -maxdepth 2 -type d

section: awk: Pattern Scanning and Processing Language
text:
awk: Pattern Scanning and Processing Language
Throughout these first three practicals, you have become familar with pattern searching and input/output streams and redirection. awk is a powerful text processing toolset that builds on these concepts, allowing for programming like operations on files and pipe input with great flexibility. While it is a full programming language, we will introduce it mostly as a tool to use when it cant be accomplished with simpler commands like grep, sed, cut, sort, and uniq. Additionally, for a lot of cases it is easier to just use a modern interpreted programming language like Python or R, but when awk is the most suitable it can do said job very well.

awk (Aho, Weinberger, and Kernighan): Allows for advanced text processing and file manipulation







Would you like to know more?





Awk programs can get quite complex, and we will not cover all its features here. However, it is a very useful tool to have in your toolbox, and I encourage you to explore it further on your own. A good resource is the GNU Awk User’s Guide.



Some key segments of an awkstatement::

-F: Specifies the input delimiter (default is whitespace)
BEGIN{}: Block of programming that runs before processing any input lines (before any text is processed)
END{}: Block that runs after processing all input lines (after all text has been processed)
{}: Block that runs for each input line (the middle block, where the main processing happens)
$1, $2, ...: Represents the first, second, etc. fields (eg. columns) in the current line
OFS: Output delimiter (default is a space, can be set in BEGIN block)

What follows here are some examples of using awk. First off awk is great for quick column selection and simple filtering:
# Print seqid and type columns of a gff file
awk -F'\t' 'BEGIN{OFS="\t"} {print $1,$3,$9}' AF316.gff > seqid_type.tsv
# This was something we also could do with cut right?
cut -f1,3,9 AF316.gff > seqid_type_cut.tsv
You can also filter rows based on conditions, to retain only specific features
#Here we can filter for only CDS features
awk -F'\t' '$3=="CDS"' AF316.gff > cds_features.tsv
# We can do something similar in grep here as well
grep "CDS" AF316.gff > cds_features_grep.tsv
Another thing is performing operations on the data in transit
# Here we can calculate the length of each CDS feature and output it as a new column
awk -F'\t' 'BEGIN{OFS="\t"} $3=="CDS"{print $1,$4,$5,$9,($5-$4+1)}' AF316.gff > cds_features_length.tsv

# Lets operate some more on the feature length file
# Calculate the total number of CDS features and their average length
awk -F'\t' 'BEGIN{OFS="\t"} {total_length+=($5-$4+1); count++} END{print "Total_CDS",count,"Average_Length",total_length/count}' cds_features_length.tsv
Here is where doing something equivalent in bash would need far more steps, likely iteratiing over the file line by line and performing calculations in a loop. This is where awk shines, as it allows for concise and efficient processing of structured text data without the need for command flows that should be a script in the first place. If you find any good awk one liners, its a good idea to keep them around for quick lookups of output data when youre running bioinformatic pipelines.

title: Practical 4: Scripts and Advanced Text Manipulation
text:
Starting a bash script
We are already familiar with bash, one of the most common shell used in Linux and macOS, and is the default shell on most HPC systems. A bash script is simply a text file containing a series of bash commands that can be executed in sequence, and is interpreted by the bash interpreter. The first line of a bash script is typically a shebang line, which tells the system which interpreter to use to execute the script. The shebang line for a bash script is #!/usr/bin/env bash.
# Start by creating a new file called process_AF_genome.sh
touch process_AF_genome.sh

# Open the file in your editor and add the shebang line at the top
#!/usr/bin/env bash

# Now change the file permissions to make it executable
chmod +x process_AF_genome.sh

# To run the script, simply run the filename in your terminal
./process_AF_genome.sh

title: Practical 4: Scripts and Advanced Text Manipulation
text:
Variables
Lets begin by adding some variables to our script, we will use these variables to store the input and output file names, as well as the gene name pattern we want to look for in our ffn files. We will also initialize a variable to store the total number of genes matching the pattern found across all files.
# For these variables, we typically use the full path to the file, this makes it easier to run the script from any directory
# Swap the paths below with the correct paths to your files
INPUT_DIR="path/to/data"
OUTPUT_DIR="path/to/output"

# You can also use variables to store parameters, such as the gene name pattern we want to look for in our ffn files
GENE_NAME_PATTERN="gene_name"

# You can also Initialize variables to store intermediate values, such as the total number of genes matching the pattern found
TOTAL_GENES_FOR_PATTERN=0

title: Practical 4: Scripts and Advanced Text Manipulation
text:
For loops
Since the ffn files we have contain a multitude of gene sequences and their headers, extracting these genes across multiple files will require repeated parsing setups. This is where for loops come in, they allow us to iterate over a list of items and execute a block of code for each item in the list. In our case, we can use a for loop to iterate over a list of input files and process each file in turn.

for: A control flow statement that allows us to iterate over a list of items and execute a block of code for each item
do and done: Keywords used to define the start and end of a loop block
basename: A command that extracts the base name of a file (the file name without the path and extension), very useful for creating output file names based on input file names

# Initiate the gene_counts.tsv file with a header
[..1..] > ${OUTPUT_DIR}/gene_counts.tsv

# In our INPUT_DIR we have multiple ffn files, a good way (if you have a good structured folder) to iterate over all ffn files is to use a for loop with a wildcard
for ffn_file in ${INPUT_DIR}/*.ffn; do 

  base_name=$(basename ${ffn_file} .ffn)
  
  grep -A 1 -E "^>${GENE_NAME_PATTERN}" "${ffn_file}" > "${OUTPUT_DIR}/${base_name}_filtered.ffn"

  gene_count=$([..2..] || true)
  TOTAL_GENES_FOR_PATTERN=$((TOTAL_GENES_FOR_PATTERN + gene_count))

  echo -e "${base_name}\t${gene_count}" >> ${OUTPUT_DIR}/gene_counts.tsv

  echo "Processed ${ffn_file}, found ${gene_count} genes matching pattern '${GENE_NAME_PATTERN}'"
done

Global set-options for debugging
Lets begin by setting the global options for our script, these are commands that define the general behaviour of our script. They will most likely always be in your scripts, and are a good starting point for debugging. A classic is the set -euo combination:

set -e: Exit immediately if a command exits with a non-zero status (i.e. as not expected)
set -u: Treat unset variables as an error when substituting (kills if you try to use a variable that has not been given a value)
set -o pipefail: Return the exit status of the last command in the pipe (if a command in a pipe fails, the whole pipe fails)

set -e  
set -u  
set -o pipefail  

# One additional setting is to add debugging output
# This will print each command before it is executed, which can be useful for debugging
# But it can also be very verbose, and clog up your output/logs
set -x

section: Custom error messages: Utilizing if/else statements for debugging
text:
Custom error messages: Utilizing if/else statements for debugging
However, they wont help with finding the exact spot where the error occurs. One way to debug your code easily, is to use echo and create custom error messages at different stages of your script. Another way is to use traps, however we will not cover that here.

if: A control flow statement that allows us to execute a block of code if a certain condition is met
then: A keyword used to define the start of an if block
else: A keyword used to define an alternative block of code if the condition is not met
fi: A keyword used to define the end of an if block

# Here is an example of a custom error message
if [ ! -f "$INPUT_FILE" ]; then
  echo "Error: Input file $INPUT_FILE does not exist."
  exit 1
fi
The placement of error messages also need to make sense, for example if you are checking for the existence of a file, it should be placed before you try to read the file. If you are checking for the number of genes found in a file, it should be placed after you have processed the file.
# The previous example makes sense to place after we assign the variable INPUT_FILE, but before we try to read the file.
# ex.
INPUT_FILE="${INPUT_DIR}/some_file.ffn"

if [ ! -f "$INPUT_FILE" ]; then
  echo "Error: Input file $INPUT_FILE does not exist."
  exit 1
fi
If we placed the conditional block before we defined INPUT_FILE, it would not make sense, as the script would fail every time. Same thing would happen if we placed it after we tried to read the file, as the script would have already failed before reaching the conditional block if the file did not exist.






Exercise: Custom error messages



Add custom error messages to your script to check for the following conditions:

Check if the input and output directories exist
Check if a name pattern is provided
Print the basename of the file being processed in the for loop
Check if any genes names matching the pattern were found in the current file







Solution:





Below are some suggestions for the custom error messages:
if [ ! -d "$INPUT_DIR" ]; then
  echo "Error: Input directory $INPUT_DIR does not exist."
  exit 1
fi
# and 
if [ ! -d "$OUTPUT_DIR" ]; then
  echo "Error: Output directory $OUTPUT_DIR does not exist."
  exit 1
fi

echo "Processing file: ${base_name}"

if [ "${gene_count}" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "Warning: No genes matching pattern '${GENE_NAME_PATTERN}' found in ${ffn_file}"
fi












OPTARGS - Adding flags to make your scripts flexible (THIS IS OPTIONAL)





Up until now, our scripts have been quite rigid - they expect specific input files and parameters; an occasionally bad habit that people refer to as “hardcoding”. However, in many scenarios, we often want our scripts to be more flexible and adaptable to different inputs and options. This is where OPTARGS comes in - a built-in bash tool that allows us to easily handle command-line options and arguments. You might recognize this from the command-line tools we’ve used so far, where we can add flags like -h for help or -v for verbose output. By using OPTARGS in our scripts, we can create flags for our own programs, making them more user-friendly and versatile.
A few key commands that we will use in this section:

getopts: A built-in bash tool for parsing command-line options and arguments
case statement: A control flow statement that allows us to execute different blocks of code based on the value of a variable

Exercises
# To begin using OPTARGS, we need to add a while loop at the top of our script to handle the options
# the OPTARG variable will hold the value of whatever comes after the flag in the command line
# A while loop iterates over the options provided to the script, and sets option variables based with the read value from the command line
while getopts "i:o:p:h" opt; do
  case $opt in
    i) INPUT_DIR="$OPTARG" ;;  # -i flag for input directory
    o) OUTPUT_DIR="$OPTARG" ;; # -o flag for output directory
    p) GENE_NAME_PATTERN="$OPTARG" ;; # -p flag for gene name pattern
    h) echo "Usage: $0 -i input_dir -o output_dir -p gene_name_pattern"  # -h flag for help
       exit 0 ;;
    *) echo "Invalid option: -$OPTARG" >&2
       exit 1 ;;
  esac
done

# We can add checks to ensure that the required options are provided
if [ -z "$INPUT_DIR" ] || [ -z "$OUTPUT_DIR" ]; then
  echo "Error: Input and output directories are required."
  echo "Usage: $0 -i input_dir -o output_dir -p gene_name_pattern"
  exit 1
fi

# Its also a good idea to set default values for optional parameters, you do this in the same way as when you set variables normally
GENE_NAME_PATTERN="${GENE_NAME_PATTERN:-gene_name}"  # Default pattern if not provided
# This sets GENE_NAME_PATTERN to the value provided by the -p flag, or to "gene_name" if no value is provided (as we did before)
Now take the script you wrote before, and modify it to use OPTARGS for input and output files as well as a pattern selection OPTARGS should be placed at the top of your script, after the shebang line and global settings Remember to test your script with different combinations of options and arguments to ensure it behaves as expected

Now that you have a finished script, try to translate it into pseudocode. Once you have written a complete pseudocode, trade with a partner and see if they can understand what your script does based on your pseudocode.









Key Takeaways




awk is a powerful tool for advanced text processing and file manipulation, it can fulfill some roles without needing to write a full script.
Writing scripts allows for structured, reproducible, and automated workflows
Variables allow for storing values that can be used multiple times in a script, making it easier to modify and maintain
For loops allow for iterating over a list of items and executing a block of code for each item, useful for processing multiple files
If/else statements allow for conditional logic in scripts, enabling different actions based on input data or parameters
Debugging is an essential skill for any programmer - use global settings, traps and custom error messages to help you find and fix errors in your code
Using OPTARGS allows you to create flexible scripts that can handle different inputs and options. It also enables other people to use your scripts more easily









Pro Tips for Scripting




Test your awk commands on the first few lines with head -5 data.csv | awk ... before running on huge files!
Use meaningful variable names (RAW_SEQUENCES not rs)
Comment your scripts - Others cant read your mind!
Test scripts on small datasets first

title: Practical 5: Software Installation and Containers
text:
Up until now youve had to make everything by yourself (sort of, at least using base programs that come with your unix distro). This approach, while flexible, defeats one of they key benefits of modern bioinformatics; Open source and collaborative solutions to large data handling. Thanks to a lot of effort, there are countless of free, open-source tools available in various repositiories on the internet.
However these tools, while saving us a lot of time, may be tricky to find and set up correctly. Different tools require different dependencies, versions, or system libraries. This often leads to complex webs of libraries and packages that act as the backbone of your code, which can be difficult to manage and reproduce on other systems. In this practical, you’ll learn where to find tools, various ways of installing an managing them (conda, apt), cloning repos from GitHub, and—most importantly—how to package tools in a Singularity/Apptainer containers that you can copy to, and run, anywhere (including HPC environments).






Learning Objectives



By the end of this practical you should be able to:

Find and identify bioinformatics tools in public repositories
Install software locally using package managers (apt, conda)
Create and manage conda environments for isolated software setups
Write a basic Singularity definition file to create a container from a base image
Build and test a Singularity container locally
Transfer and run a Singularity container on an HPC using SLURM

Setting up Conda
To begin with, we will install Miniconda, a minimal installer for Conda. Conda is an open-source package management system and environment management system that runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It quickly installs, runs, and updates packages and their dependencies. Conda also creates, saves, loads, and switches between environments on your local computer.
